import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 477

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/477](https://www.erdosproblems.com/477)
- [Sek59](http://dml.cz/dmlcz/100376) Milan Sekanina, Замечания к фактoризации беcкoнечнoй цикличеcкoй группы, Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal, Vol. 9 (1959), No. 4, 485–495
-/

open Polynomial Set

namespace Erdos477

/--
Is there a polynomial $f:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$ of degree at least $2$ and a set
$A\subset \mathbb{Z}$ such that for any $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ there is exactly one $a\in A$ and
$b\in \{ f(k) : k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ such that $n=a+b$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ f : ℤ[X], 2 ≤ f.degree ∧ ∃ A : Set ℤ,
      ∀ z, ∃! ab ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = ab.1 + ab.2 := by
  sorry

/--
There is no such $A$ for the polynomial $f(x) = X^2$.

This is shown in [Sek59].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.S_sq :
    letI f := X ^ 2
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
There is no such $A$ for any polynomial $f(x) = aX^2 + bX + c$, if $a | b$
with $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$.
This was found be AlphaProof for the specific instance $X^2 - X + 1$ and then generalised.
 -/
@[category research solved, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.degree_two_dvd_condition_b_ne_zero {a b c : ℤ} (ha : a ≠ 0) (hb : b ≠ 0)
    (hab : a ∣ b) :
    let f := a • X ^ 2 + b • X + C c
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
Probably there is no such $A$ for the polynomial $X^3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.X_pow_three :
    letI f := X ^ 3
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

/--
Probably there is no such $A$ for the polynomial $X^k$ for any $k \ge 2$. This is asked in [Sek59].
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem erdos_477.variants.monomial (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    letI f := X ^ k
    ∀ A : Set ℤ, ∃ z, ¬ ∃! a ∈ A ×ˢ (Set.range f.eval), z = a.1 + a.2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos477

findings.description: The docstring's attribution “This is asked in [Sek59]” needs qualification. Sekanina asks about powers of nonnegative integers, whereas `Set.range f.eval` here uses all integer arguments. For odd k these are different value sets: the Lean set includes negative powers. The Lean statement remains the natural monomial subcase of the all-integer problem on the currently cited Erdős webpage; this finding concerns the precise attribution, not a claim that the two tiling problems have been proved inequivalent.
findings.source_evidence: Sekanina (1959), p.485 defines his set of nonnegative integers; p.490, immediately after Remark 1.7, says that the case M consisting of their kth powers, k > 2, remains unresolved. https://dml.cz/bitstream/handle/10338.dmlcz/100376/CzechMathJ_09-1959-4_2.pdf
findings.suggested_fix: Qualify the docstring: this is the all-integer monomial subcase of the webpage's formulation, while Sekanina asks the analogous question for nonnegative powers. If adding Sekanina's exact variant, use `Set.range (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℤ) ^ k)`.

status_issues.source_status: The current Erdős webpage marks the problem SOLVED and records a positive answer. It attributes constructions independently to GPT prompted by Price and pipeline-math, and states that a complement exists for f(n)=n^d for every even d≥6. The page was last edited 5 September 2026.
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/477: “contrary to the expectation of Erdős and Graham, such an A does exist whenever f(n)=n^d for all even d≥6.” The linked pipeline-math paper additionally states an all-integer thirteenth-power construction in Theorem 1.1.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to `research solved`, replace `answer(sorry)` with `answer(True)`, and cite the construction.

status_issues.recorded: `@[category research open]`, asserting nonexistence of a complement for every k≥2.
status_issues.source_status: The universal negative conjecture has been disproved: the current source records complements for every even exponent d≥6, so k=6 already contradicts the universal assertion.
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/477, updated 5 September 2026, explicitly records the even-d≥6 constructions. The linked pipeline-math paper also gives a counterexample at k=13 using all integer arguments.
status_issues.suggested_change: Record the universal conjecture as disproved and tag it `research solved`, for example using `answer(False) ↔ (∀ k : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → ...)` with the quantifiers inside the proposition, or state an explicit positive counterexample. Keep unresolved individual degrees as separate open variants.

reformulations.difference: Lean represents the polynomial by `ℤ[X]`, whereas the prose `f : ℤ → ℤ` can also be read as allowing rational-coefficient integer-valued polynomials.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This does not change the existential question. An integer-valued polynomial has rational coefficients, by interpolation at integer points. Choose a positive common denominator d and put g = d f ∈ ℤ[X], of the same degree. If A and B = f(ℤ) uniquely sum to ℤ, then dA + {0,…,d−1} and dB = g(ℤ) uniquely sum to ℤ, by the quotient–remainder decomposition. The reverse existential implication is immediate since integer-coefficient polynomials are integer-valued. The set-level equivalence between tileability of B and dB was proved in dilation.lean; the full polynomial-existential equivalence was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: Lean evaluates the square polynomial on all integers; Sekanina indexes squares by nonnegative integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The value sets are identical: every integer square equals the square of its natural absolute value, and every nonnegative integer is an integer. Consequently the two nonexistence statements are equivalent. Both the range equality and the full statement equivalence were proved in scratch.lean.

review.notes: All five declarations were checked. No definite mathematical misformalization was found. The scratch files `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` and `/workspace/review/dilation.lean` compile without errors; their test proofs do not use the problem's sorry-backed theorems. Checks covered bounded uniqueness, uniqueness of values rather than polynomial arguments, the negated-existence formulation, empty A, nonempty polynomial images, exclusion of degrees 0 and 1, k=2, and the quadratic's evaluation and degree. One source distinction is worth preserving: the original Erdős–Graham book uses S={f(1),f(2),…}, while the current explicitly cited webpage uses f(ℤ). The main declaration follows the webpage exactly; I have not treated these input-domain conventions as an established equivalent reindexing.
